design_detail: Retrospective cohort study in the MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims database, 2013–2017 (about 12 million enrollees a year). Adults aged 18–64 who began a new buprenorphine episode (no buprenorphine claim in the previous 60 days), stayed on it continuously for at least 180 days, then stopped (a gap of more than 60 days beyond the days supplied; the last day of medication coverage counts as the day of stopping) and stayed enrolled for 6 months afterwards. The 8,996 people were grouped by how long they had stayed on buprenorphine (6–9, 9–12, 12–15 and 15–18 months). Outcomes in the 6 months after stopping: any emergency department visit, any inpatient admission, any filled full-agonist opioid prescription, and any medically treated drug overdose (opioid or non-opioid). Logistic regressions compared each longer group with the 6–9-month group, adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, Medicaid plan type, psychiatric, alcohol and non-opioid drug use diagnoses, and initial buprenorphine dose. There is no group that stayed on buprenorphine. Appraised with ROBINS-I as a non-randomized comparison of treatment durations, as the round brief directs. Read from the online-first version (AJP in Advance).
can_establish: How often Medicaid enrollees who stopped buprenorphine after 6 to 18 months of continuous treatment had emergency visits, hospital admissions, full-agonist opioid prescriptions and medically treated overdoses in the next 6 months, and whether those who had stayed longer differed on these outcomes after adjustment for recorded characteristics.
cannot_establish: Whether stopping buprenorphine raises the risk of overdose compared with staying on it (no group that continued), whether longer treatment causes the better outcomes (people stopped at different times for reasons not recorded), how many overdoses were fatal (deaths are not recorded and people who died lost enrolment and were excluded), or whether the figures apply to people who stop in the first weeks or months, or outside Medicaid.

sample.recruitment: Registry: insurance claims and enrolment records of the MarketScan multistate Medicaid database, 2013–2017, including inpatient, outpatient, emergency and pharmacy claims billed to Medicaid (Methods, Study Design and Participants, 1st paragraph, PDF p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 18–64 at initiation; a new episode after a 60-day baseline without buprenorphine claims; formulations approved for pain excluded; continuous buprenorphine for 180 to 545 days by days supplied; discontinuation within the study window, defined as a gap of more than 60 days beyond the days supplied; continuous Medicaid enrolment for 6 months after stopping; initiation before 1 January 2017 (Methods, PDF pp. 2–3; Figure 1 note, PDF p. 2). Flow: 26,576 with a continuous episode of more than 6 months; 10,481 who did not stop and 3,159 who stopped with less than 6 months left in the study window removed (12,936); 3,940 without continuous enrolment through the follow-up removed (8,996) (Results, 1st paragraph, PDF pp. 3–4; Figure 2, PDF p. 3).
sample.demographics: 61.0% women; 76.4% aged 25–44; 91.5% White; mean initial dose 8.0 mg/day (group means 7.9–8.2) (Results, 1st–2nd paragraphs, PDF pp. 3–4; Table 1, PDF p. 4). From the Table 1 totals (editors' calculation): psychiatric diagnosis 30.9%, alcohol use disorder 4.8%, non-opioid drug use disorder 21.7%.
sample.attrition: 3,940 of the 12,936 who stopped within the window (30.5%, editors' calculation) were excluded because they were not continuously enrolled in the 6 months after stopping; excluded and included people are not compared (Results, 1st paragraph, PDF pp. 3–4; Figure 2).
sample.selection_effects: Only people who reached 6 months of continuous treatment, whom the authors describe as a minority of Medicaid patients who start buprenorphine and as likely relatively stable (Discussion, 7th paragraph, PDF p. 6), and only those who stopped: 10,481 of 26,576 with such an episode (39.4%, editors' calculation) had not stopped and were excluded. The 6-month enrolment requirement after stopping removes people who died or lost Medicaid in that period; the authors state that people with fatal overdoses would have lost eligibility and been ineligible (PDF pp. 6–7). People also covered by Medicare were excluded (PDF p. 7).

exposure.measurement: Pharmacy claims: days supplied of buprenorphine formulations approved for opioid use disorder, from the index claim to the last fill before a gap of more than 60 days (Methods, Study Design and Participants, 3rd paragraph, PDF p. 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Duration groups by days supplied: 180–270, 271–364, 365–455 and 456–545 days (PDF p. 3). Initial dose recorded only as a group mean (7.9–8.2 mg/day; Table 1); formulation, later doses and whether medication was taken are not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded only as diagnoses on the day of initiation or in the 60-day baseline: alcohol use disorder (ICD-10 F10) and non-opioid drug use disorders (F12–F16, F18–F19), both adjusted for; actual drug use not measured (Methods, Measures, 2nd paragraph, PDF p. 3).

comparison.controls: The 6–9-month group (n=4,126) is the reference for the 9–12, 12–15 and 15–18-month groups; no group continued buprenorphine (Figure 1 note, PDF p. 2; Methods, Statistical Analysis, PDF p. 3).
comparison.matching: None; regression adjustment for age group, sex, race/ethnicity (White or nonwhite), Medicaid plan type, psychiatric diagnosis, alcohol use disorder, non-opioid drug use disorder and initial buprenorphine dose (PDF p. 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Addiction severity, which the authors could not measure from claims (Discussion, 7th paragraph, PDF p. 6), reasons for stopping (planned taper, dropping out, cost or coverage limits, incarceration, moving), opioid use, housing and employment, and treatment after stopping (restarting buprenorphine, methadone, naltrexone).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The same diagnostic covariates for all groups.

outcomes.instruments: Claims in the 6 months after the last day of medication coverage: at least one all-cause emergency department visit; at least one all-cause inpatient admission; at least one filled full-agonist opioid prescription; at least one medically treated drug overdose, opioid or non-opioid, by ICD-10 codes printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50, with the full list in Table S1 of the online supplement, which was not among the files (Methods, Measures, 1st paragraph, PDF p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not reported. Claims capture only overdoses that reached billed care; deaths outside hospital are not captured.
outcomes.operationalization: Each outcome is binary (any event in 6 months). Full-agonist opioid prescriptions are read as a marker of relapse or poorly coordinated care (PDF p. 3), although they may also be prescribed for pain.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 4 outcomes by 3 duration comparisons (12 adjusted odds ratios) at p<0.05, plus a sensitivity analysis.

analysis.effect_sizes: Unadjusted 6-month rates across the four groups: emergency visits 41.2–48.6%, inpatient admissions 11.3–13.9%, full-agonist opioid prescriptions 19.1–25.9%, medically treated overdoses 5.1–5.5%; overall, 464 of 8,996 (5.2%) had at least one overdose (Results, 3rd–4th paragraphs, PDF p. 4). 15–18 against 6–9 months, unadjusted: emergency visits 41.2% vs 48.6% (p<0.001), admissions 11.3% vs 13.9% (p<0.05), opioid prescriptions 19.1% vs 25.9% (p<0.001) (Results, 4th paragraph, PDF p. 4). Adjusted odds ratios (Table 2, PDF p. 6): 15–18 months, admissions 0.79 (95% CI 0.64–0.99), emergency visits 0.75 (0.65–0.86), overdose 1.04 (0.75–1.44), opioid prescriptions 0.67 (0.56–0.80); 12–15 months, 0.86 (0.72–1.03), 0.84 (0.75–0.95), 1.10 (0.84–1.43), 0.84 (0.73–0.97); 9–12 months, 0.86 (0.74–1.01), 0.94 (0.85–1.04), 1.04 (0.82–1.30), 0.95 (0.85–1.07). Sensitivity analysis with a documented opioid use disorder diagnosis (N=8,077), 15–18 against 6–9 months: emergency visits 0.74 (0.64–0.86), admissions 0.79 (0.63–0.99), opioid prescriptions 0.68 (0.56–0.82); overdose odds equivalent across groups, overall rate 5.6% (Results, 6th paragraph, PDF p. 5). Editors' calculation from the printed unadjusted rates, 15–18 against 6–9 months: 7.4 percentage points fewer with an emergency visit, 2.6 fewer admitted, 6.8 fewer with an opioid prescription; overdose 464/8,996 = 5.2% (Wilson 95% CI 4.7–5.6%).
analysis.covariates: Age group, sex, race/ethnicity, Medicaid plan type (fee for service or capitation), psychiatric diagnosis (ICD-10 F01–F09, F20–F99), alcohol use disorder, non-opioid drug use disorder, and initial buprenorphine dose as a continuous variable (Methods, PDF p. 3; Table 2, PDF p. 6).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. The authors state that the 3-month groupings were chosen before the analyses and that their hypothesis was set before the data were analysed (PDF pp. 2–3).
analysis.selective_reporting: All four primary outcomes are reported for all three comparisons (Table 2), and the null overdose result is in the abstract. The abstract's range for emergency visits (42.1–49.9%) differs from the Results (41.2–48.6%). Rates for the 9–12 and 12–15-month groups are shown only as bars in Figure 3; Tables S1–S3 are in the online supplement.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors suggest that the null overdose result may reflect insufficient power (Discussion, 4th paragraph, PDF p. 5). The interval for the 15–18-month group (0.75–1.44) is compatible with odds of overdose 25% lower to 44% higher.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 8,996 Medicaid enrollees who stopped buprenorphine after 6 to 18 months and remained enrolled for 6 more months, 41–49% had an emergency visit, 11–14% a hospital admission, 19–26% a full-agonist opioid prescription and 5.2% at least one medically treated overdose in those 6 months. People who had stayed 15–18 months had lower adjusted odds of emergency visits, admissions and opioid prescriptions than those who stopped after 6–9 months, and the same odds of overdose.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the risk of acute care and overdose was high after stopping, whatever the duration, and that superior outcomes became significant beyond 15 months of treatment (abstract, PDF p. 1); but the study has no group that continued treatment, and the 12–15-month group already had significantly lower odds of emergency visits and opioid prescriptions (Table 2, PDF p. 6). The discussion says the study demonstrates that the period after stopping goes with overdose rates about two to three times those of a general sample of people with opioid use disorder (Discussion, 4th paragraph, PDF p. 5), citing a meta-analysis of death rates per 1000 person-years (reference 29, Sordo et al., 2017) without giving the figures compared or how a 6-month proportion of medically treated overdoses was made comparable. The authors' statement that fatal overdoses are unlikely to differ between groups (PDF p. 6) cannot be checked, since people who died were excluded by design. The conclusions concede that the design cannot establish a causal relationship (PDF p. 7), yet recommend longer treatment and changes to insurance and care systems.

timeline.event: Pennsylvania Medicaid cohort (Gordon et al., 2015, as cited): 21% persistently refilled buprenorphine for 12 months; against people who persisted only 3–5 months, they had an 18% lower risk of hospitalization and a 14% lower risk of emergency department use (Discussion, 6th paragraph, PDF p. 6).
Meta-analysis of mortality during and after opioid substitution treatment, cited for the claim that overdose rates after stopping are two to three times those of a general sample

Cohort after non-fatal overdose (Larochelle et al., 2018, as cited): an approximate annual rate of 5% to 7.5% for subsequent overdoses, with which the authors compare their 6-month rate (Discussion, 5th paragraph, PDF p. 5).

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication is described in the paper or known from the files read for this card. The finding that about 5 in 100 had a medically treated overdose within 6 months of stopping comes from one claims database and excludes deaths; whether stopping raises overdose risk compared with continuing needs studies that link deaths and include people who continue.

funding.funder: NIDA grants K23 DA044342, T32 DA031099 and 1R01 DA047347-01; Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality grants R18 HS03258, U19 HS021112 and R18HS02346; NIH National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences award UL1TR003017 (Author and article information, PDF p. 7).
funding.declared_conflicts: Dr. Samples has received consulting fees from the American Society for Addiction Medicine; the other authors report no financial relationships with commercial interests (PDF p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University and from Rutgers University. The paper argues for longer treatment and for insurance and care-system changes, and cites the authors' earlier work on a treatment cascade, quality measures and discontinuation (references 3, 5, 16 and 31). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort that links treatment or claims records to death records, so that fatal overdoses are counted and people are not lost when their insurance ends, comparing people who stop buprenorphine with similar people who continue over the same calendar time, with reasons for stopping and later treatment recorded; or a randomized trial of continued treatment against a planned taper after a set duration, with overdose and death as outcomes.

domains.note: Duration was not assigned: people who stop after 6–9 months may differ in severity, stability, circumstances and reasons for stopping. Adjustment covers only demographics, plan type, initial dose and diagnoses recorded at baseline; no measure of severity (the authors say none was available, PDF p. 6) and no time-varying factors.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Entry required stopping within the window and then 6 months of continuous enrolment after stopping, a condition observed after the start of follow-up: anyone who died, including from overdose, or lost Medicaid in those 6 months was excluded.

Duration and the date of stopping are derived from fill dates and days supplied with a 60-day gap rule; fills do not show whether medication was taken, and restarting after the gap within the outcome window is not described.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Treatment after stopping (restarting buprenorphine, methadone or naltrexone) is not reported and may differ between groups.

3,940 of 12,936 (30.5%) were excluded for incomplete enrolment in the outcome period; loss of enrolment can follow death, a direct consequence of the outcome; excluded and included people are not compared.

Claims-based outcomes do not depend on knowledge of the group, but capture only billed events; fatal overdoses outside hospital are missed; the printed overdose codes omit T40.0–T40.4 (see reporting issues); opioid prescriptions may reflect pain care.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: All four outcomes are reported for all comparisons, including the null result for overdose, and the groupings were set before analysis (PDF p. 3).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The 6-month rates are reliable descriptions of the people included (Medicaid enrollees who stopped after at least 6 months and stayed enrolled for 6 more), but they are not the full risk after stopping, because deaths and loss of Medicaid removed people from the analysis. The comparison between durations is open to confounding by why and when people stopped. The study may be cited for how common emergency care, full-agonist opioid prescriptions and medically treated overdoses were in the 6 months after stopping long-term buprenorphine in this population, and for the absence of a detectable difference in overdose by duration; it cannot be cited for overdose risk after stopping compared with continuing, for fatal overdose, or for longer treatment causing better outcomes.

key_findings.finding: Cohort: 8,996 Medicaid enrollees aged 18–64 (MarketScan multistate claims, 2013–2017) who stopped buprenorphine after at least 180 days of continuous treatment and stayed enrolled for 6 months afterwards: 4,126 had been treated 6–9 months, 2,440 for 9–12 months, 1,499 for 12–15 months and 931 for 15–18 months.
key_findings.locator: Methods, Study Design and Participants, 1st–3rd paragraphs (pp. 2–3); Figure 2 (p. 3); Results, 2nd paragraph and Table 1 (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Of 26,576 people with a new continuous buprenorphine episode of more than 6 months, 10,481 did not stop and 3,159 stopped with less than 6 months left in the study window; of the remaining 12,936, 3,940 were excluded because they were not continuously enrolled through the 6 months after stopping.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (starts p. 3, continues p. 4); Figure 2 (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: The people included were 61.0% women, 76.4% aged 25–44 and 91.5% White; the mean initial buprenorphine dose was 8.0 mg/day (group means 7.9–8.2 mg/day); nonwhite people were slightly less likely to be in the 15–18-month group (p=0.04).

In the 6 months after stopping, across the four duration groups, 41.2–48.6% had an emergency department visit, 11.3–13.9% an inpatient admission, 19.1–25.9% filled a full-agonist opioid prescription, and 5.1–5.5% had at least one medically treated overdose.
key_findings.note: The abstract (PDF p. 1) gives 42.1–49.9% for emergency visits (see reporting issues). Overdoses counted are those of people still enrolled 6 months after stopping.

key_findings.finding: Overall, 464 of 8,996 people (5.2%) had at least one medically treated overdose (opioid or non-opioid) in the 6 months after stopping buprenorphine; overdose was not related to how long they had been treated (6 to 18 months).

Unadjusted, the 15–18-month group had fewer emergency visits (41.2% vs 48.6%, p<0.001), admissions (11.3% vs 13.9%, p<0.05) and opioid prescription claims (19.1% vs 25.9%, p<0.001) than the 6–9-month group; overdose was comparable across all groups.

Adjusted odds ratios against the 6–9-month group: 15–18 months, emergency visits 0.75 (95% CI 0.65–0.86), admissions 0.79 (0.64–0.99), opioid prescriptions 0.67 (0.56–0.80), overdose 1.04 (0.75–1.44); 12–15 months, emergency visits 0.84 (0.75–0.95) and opioid prescriptions 0.84 (0.73–0.97), admissions 0.86 (0.72–1.03), overdose 1.10 (0.84–1.43); 9–12 months, no significant difference (overdose 1.04, 0.82–1.30).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (starts p. 4, continues p. 5); Table 2 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: In the same models, overdose after stopping was less likely in women (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.54–0.79) and more likely with a psychiatric diagnosis (1.61, 1.32–1.96), alcohol use disorder (2.02, 1.47–2.79) or a non-opioid drug use disorder (1.51, 1.22–1.86); initial dose was not related (1.00 per mg, 0.97–1.04).

Restricted to the 8,077 people with a documented opioid use disorder diagnosis, the 15–18-month group again had lower odds of emergency visits (0.74, 0.64–0.86), admissions (0.79, 0.63–0.99) and opioid prescriptions (0.68, 0.56–0.82); overdose odds were equivalent across groups, with 5.6% overall having an overdose in the 6 months after stopping.

Limitations stated by the authors: no data on vital status, so fatal and non-fatal overdoses could not be told apart; people who died of overdose during treatment or in the 6 months after stopping would have lost Medicaid eligibility and were therefore not in the analysis; residual confounding is possible and addiction severity could not be measured; results are limited to Medicaid enrollees without Medicare, and the states contributing data are not named.

Stopping was defined as a gap of more than 60 days beyond the days supplied by the last fill, dated to the last day of medication coverage, so the 6-month outcome window includes the first 60 days without a buprenorphine fill.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 note (p. 2); Methods, Study Design and Participants, 3rd paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Medically treated overdose was defined by ICD-10 codes printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50 (opioid and non-opioid), with the full list in Table S1 of the online supplement; a full-agonist opioid prescription is described as generally contraindicated with buprenorphine and as a marker of relapse or poorly coordinated care.
key_findings.note: See reporting issues on the printed code range; Table S1 was not among the files.

key_findings.finding: The discussion states that overdose rates after stopping were about two to three times those observed in a general sample of people with opioid use disorder (reference 29), giving no figures for that comparison, and that the overdose rate in the sample lay within an approximate annual rate of 5% to 7.5% for subsequent overdoses reported for people with a past-year overdose (reference 2).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 42.1–49.9% for emergency department visits; the Results give 41.2–48.6%, matching the bars of Figure 3.

The abstract and conclusions place the benefit of longer treatment beyond 15 months (a minimum of 15–18 months), but the 12–15-month group already had significantly lower adjusted odds of emergency visits (0.84, 0.75–0.95) and opioid prescriptions (0.84, 0.73–0.97).
reporting_issues.consequence: The threshold of 15 months is a simplification; the data show a gradient for two outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says opioid prescription claims averaged more than 25% across groups, but the Results range is 19.1–25.9%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' reading of Figure 3 (bars calibrated on the gridlines; about 25.9%, 25.2%, 23.0% and 19.2%) gives a weighted average of about 24.5%; the statement slightly overstates the rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The overdose code list is printed as T36–T39, T40.5–T50 although the same sentence says opioid overdoses were counted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' note: in ICD-10, T40.0–T40.4 are the codes for poisoning by opium, heroin, other opioids, methadone and other synthetic narcotics, so the printed range would leave out opioid overdoses. Probably a typesetting error; Table S1 of the online supplement (not among the files) gives the codes used and should be read before the overdose figure is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The limitations say that fatal and non-fatal overdoses could not be told apart, and also that people who died of overdose would have lost eligibility and been excluded; the authors then reason that fatal overdoses are unlikely to differ between groups because overdoses occurred at similar rates.
reporting_issues.consequence: The overdoses counted are mostly those of people who survived and stayed enrolled; fatal overdoses after stopping are largely outside the data, and their distribution by group cannot be inferred from non-fatal ones.

reporting_issues.issue: The claim that overdose rates after stopping are about two to three times those of a general sample of people with opioid use disorder gives no figures; its source (reference 29, Sordo et al., 2017) pooled death rates per 1000 person-years (card sc_sordo_2017), whereas this study counts medically treated overdoses, fatal or not, as a 6-month proportion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison cannot be checked and compares different outcomes; it should not be cited as a finding of this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The 6-month overdose proportion (5.2%) is compared with annual rates of 5% to 7.5% after a past-year overdose.
reporting_issues.consequence: A 6-month proportion compared with annual rates understates the comparison; no adjustment for the length of follow-up is made.
